questions.question: The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) is computed and published by the Central Statistical Organisation (CSO) on a monthly basis. For the calculation of the index, which of the following financial years is taken as the base year?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2011-12**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Index of Industrial Production (IIP)** is a measure of the growth in the industrial sector of an economy. It is compiled and published monthly by the **Central Statistical Organisation (CSO)** under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.
 
• The IIP tracks production data from sectors like **mining, manufacturing, and electricity**, offering insights into economic activity and industrial performance.
 
• The base year used for calculating the Index of Industrial Production is **2011-12**. The base year is periodically updated to reflect structural changes in the economy and ensure the index remains relevant.
 
• The choice of 2011-12 as the base year was made to align with internationally accepted practices and improve the accuracy of the index.
 
• The IIP helps policymakers and analysts in **monitoring industrial trends**, planning economic strategies, and assessing economic health.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Components of IIP:**

 
 
• The IIP includes data from three major sectors: **Mining (14.37% weightage), Manufacturing (77.63% weightage), and Electricity (7.99% weightage)**.
 
• The highest weightage is given to the manufacturing sector due to its significant contribution to industrial activity.
 
 
 
• **Base Year Revision:**
 
 
• The base year of IIP is periodically revised to incorporate changes in industrial patterns, technology, and economic structure.
 
• The last revision was made to shift the base year from **2004-05 to 2011-12**.
 
 
 
• **Uses of IIP:**
 
 
• IIP is used by the government and economists to **assess industrial performance** and its contribution to overall economic growth.
 
• It serves as an indicator for planning fiscal and monetary policies.
 
• Investors and businesses use IIP data to understand market trends and forecast industrial demand.
 
 
 
• **Limitations of IIP:**
 
 
• IIP primarily tracks production data and does not account for **services or informal sectors**.
 
• It may not fully capture the impact of structural changes in industries due to its focus on selected items.
 
 
 
• **Related Indices:**
 
 
• The **Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI)** complements IIP by providing insights into manufacturing and service sector activities through surveys.
 
• The **Consumer Price Index (CPI)** and **Wholesale Price Index (WPI)** are other economic indices that focus on inflation and pricing trends.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Base Year Significance:** The base year is crucial as it serves as a reference point for comparing production volumes and assessing growth trends.
 
• **Sectoral Weightage:** The manufacturing sector has the highest weightage in IIP due to its predominant role in industrial growth.
 
• **Policy Implications:** IIP data is vital for designing policies that aim to improve industrial productivity and economic competitiveness.
 
• **Revision Practices:** Periodic revisions ensure that the IIP remains relevant to current economic conditions and industrial practices.
 
• **Global Comparisons:** Many countries have similar indices, such as the Industrial Production Index in the USA, which helps in global economic comparisons.

__
 
• **Sex ratio** is a demographic metric used to measure the number of **females per 1000 males** in a population.
 
• The **Census of India** adopts the practice of calculating sex ratio per 1000 males, which is widely utilized for comparative purposes and understanding gender distribution.
 
• The sex ratio is an important indicator of **gender equality** in a society and is used to assess the socio-economic conditions of the population.
 
• India's sex ratio has been a subject of concern due to factors like **preference for male children**, gender-based discrimination, and **female foeticide.**
 
• As per the **Census of India 2011**, the sex ratio stood at **940 females per 1000 males**, showing gradual improvement compared to previous decades.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Historical Trends:**

 
 
• India's sex ratio has traditionally been skewed due to **socio-cultural practices** favoring male children.
 
• In **1901**, the sex ratio was **972 females per 1000 males**, but it declined steadily over the years.
 
 
 
• **Global Comparison:**
 
 
• The global average sex ratio is approximately **984 females per 1000 males**, indicating better gender balance in many countries compared to India.
 
• Countries like **Sweden** and **Norway** have higher sex ratios due to better gender equality and healthcare systems.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiatives:**
 
 
• To address the imbalance, the Indian government launched schemes like **Beti Bachao Beti Padhao** in **2015** to promote **female child welfare**.
 
• Programs focusing on **education, healthcare, and financial inclusion** for women have been implemented to improve the sex ratio.
 
 
 
• **Implications of Skewed Sex Ratio:**
 
 
• A low sex ratio can lead to social issues such as **forced marriages**, **human trafficking**, and increased crimes against women.
 
• It can also impact the **workforce dynamics** and **economic growth** due to reduced female participation.
 
 
 
• **Regional Variations:**
 
 
• In **Kerala**, the sex ratio is one of the highest in India at **1084 females per 1000 males** (Census 2011).
 
• States like **Haryana** and **Punjab** have traditionally recorded lower sex ratios due to **gender-based practices**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) Recommendations:**

 
 
• UNFPA emphasizes the need for **gender-sensitive policies** to address disparities in sex ratios.
 
• Improvement in **female literacy rates** and **access to healthcare** are key measures suggested.
 
 
 
• **Census Data Usage:**
 
 
• Census data is crucial for planning and implementing **gender-specific policies**.
 
• It helps to identify areas requiring intervention for **women empowerment**.
 
 
 
• **Education and Awareness:**
 
 
• Promoting **education** and **awareness campaigns** can help reduce gender discrimination and improve sex ratios.
 
• Encouraging community participation is vital for addressing cultural biases.
 
 
 
• **Role of NGOs:**
 
 
• Non-governmental organizations play a significant role in **advocating gender equality** and providing support to marginalized women.

__
 
• The **Great Stupa of Sanchi** is located in the state of **Madhya Pradesh**, India, specifically in the **Raisen district**.
 
• It is one of the oldest stone structures in India, originally commissioned by Emperor **Ashoka the Great** in the **3rd century BCE**.
 
• The Stupa is a significant Buddhist architectural structure and symbolizes the burial mound of Buddha, containing **relics of the Buddha**.
 
• Sanchi is recognized as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since **1989**, highlighting its cultural and historical importance.
 
• The site consists of a group of Buddhist monuments, including **monasteries, temples, and stupas**, which showcase the evolution of Buddhist art and architecture over centuries.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• The construction of the Great Stupa was initiated by Emperor **Ashoka** after he embraced Buddhism and sought to promote Buddhist teachings.
 
• The site contains relics of the Buddha and serves as a place of meditation and devotion for followers of Buddhism.
 
• Later rulers, including the **Shungas** and **Satavahanas**, contributed to the Stupa’s expansion and embellishment, adding gateways and sculptures.
 
 
 
• **Architectural Features:**
 
 
• The Great Stupa has a hemispherical dome built on a platform, symbolizing the **world mountain**.
 
• It is surrounded by a circular path for **pradakshina (circumambulation)**, a common practice in Buddhist rituals.
 
• The four intricately carved gateways, known as **toranas**, represent various events of Buddha’s life and teachings.
 
• The Stupa also features a **chatra (umbrella-like structure)** at the top, signifying honor and protection.
 
 
 
• **Religious Significance:**
 
 
• The Stupa represents **Buddhist philosophy**, symbolizing the path to enlightenment and the cycle of life, death, and rebirth.
 
• It is considered one of the most important pilgrimage sites for **Buddhists**, attracting devotees from around the world.
 
 
 
• **Madhya Pradesh as a Cultural Hub:**
 
 
• Madhya Pradesh is known for its rich cultural heritage, including other historic sites like **Khajuraho Temples** and the **Bhimbetka Rock Shelters**.
 
• The state plays a significant role in showcasing India’s ancient history and traditions.

• **UNESCO World Heritage Status:**

 
 
• The Sanchi Stupa was designated as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** in **1989** due to its outstanding cultural significance.
 
• The site is protected by the **Archaeological Survey of India**.
 
 
 
• **Other Sites in Sanchi:**

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a constitutional post in India
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Solicitor General**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Solicitor General** of India is not a constitutional post as it is not mentioned in the **Constitution of India**. It is a statutory position and part of the legal system to assist the Attorney General.
 
• The **Attorney General of India**, on the other hand, is a constitutional post mentioned under **Article 76** of the Constitution and serves as the chief legal advisor to the Government of India.
 
• The **Comptroller and Auditor-General of India (CAG)** is a constitutional authority established under **Article 148** of the Constitution, responsible for auditing government accounts and ensuring accountability.
 
• The **Advocate General** in a state is also a constitutional post mentioned under **Article 165**. The Advocate General acts as the chief legal advisor to the state government.
 
• While the Solicitor General assists the Attorney General in performing legal duties, it is not a constitutional position and does not have a direct mention in the Constitution of India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Attorney General of India:**

 
 
• The Attorney General is appointed by the President under **Article 76** of the Constitution.
 
• He/She must be qualified to be appointed as a judge of the Supreme Court.
 
• The Attorney General represents the Government of India in legal matters and provides legal advice to the President and other union ministers.
 
 
 
• **Comptroller and Auditor-General of India (CAG):**
 
 
• The CAG is appointed by the President under **Article 148** of the Constitution.

questions.question: The working of lactometers is based on:

• **Archimedes' Principle** states that when an object is partially or fully immersed in a fluid, it experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by it.
 
• **Lactometers** are devices used to measure the density of milk. They work based on this principle as the buoyant force acting on the lactometer depends on the density of milk.
 
• The lactometer floats more in milk with higher density and sinks further in milk with lower density, helping determine the quality of milk.
 
• Archimedes' Principle is widely used in various applications such as designing ships, submarines, and other floating objects. *Hence, the correct answer is Archimedes' Principle.*
 
• This principle is fundamental to fluid mechanics and has numerous practical applications across different fields of science and engineering.

• **Shipbuilding:** The principle is used to design ships that float by ensuring their weight is balanced by the displaced water's weight.

• **Mendel’s Principle:** Refers to the fundamental laws of inheritance in genetics. It does not apply to fluid mechanics or lactometers.
 
• **Boyle’s Law:** States that the pressure of a gas is inversely proportional to its volume at constant temperature. It is not relevant to the functioning of lactometers.

questions.question: In an ideal pyramid of energy, if 500 Joule (J) of solar energy is received by green plants, then only ______ will be trapped by plants and the rest will be lost to the environment.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**5 J**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In an **ideal pyramid of energy**, energy transfer between trophic levels follows the **10% rule**, meaning only about **10%** of the energy is passed to the next level, while the remaining **90%** is lost as heat or used for metabolic processes.
 
• When **500 J** of solar energy is received by the **green plants** (producers), only **10% of this energy** is trapped and converted into chemical energy via photosynthesis.
 
• Thus, the energy trapped by green plants will be **10% of 500 J**, which is equal to **5 J**.
 
• The remaining **495 J** is lost to the environment in the form of heat, respiration, and other non-usable forms of energy.
 
• This phenomenon highlights the inefficiency of energy transfer in ecological systems. *Hence, the correct answer is 5 J.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Energy Pyramid:**

 
 
• The energy pyramid is a graphical representation of the flow of energy through different trophic levels in an ecosystem.
 
• It follows the principle that **energy decreases** as it moves from producers to consumers (primary, secondary, tertiary).
 
• Energy is measured in units such as **joules (J)** or calories.
 
• Producers form the base of the pyramid, capturing solar energy through photosynthesis.
 
 
 
• **10% Rule:**
 
 
• The **10% rule** states that only about **10%** of the energy at one trophic level is passed to the next level.
 
• The rest of the energy is lost as **heat**, used for **metabolism**, or excreted.
 
• This explains why higher trophic levels have less energy and fewer organisms.
 
 
 
• **Green Plants:**
 
 
• Green plants are **primary producers** that capture solar energy and convert it into chemical energy via **photosynthesis**.
 
• They serve as the base of the food chain and provide energy to primary consumers.
 
• The efficiency of energy conversion in plants is influenced by factors such as **light intensity, temperature, and availability of nutrients.**
 
 
 
• **Energy Loss:**
 
 
• Energy is lost at each trophic level due to **heat loss during respiration**, incomplete digestion, and excretion.
 
• Only a fraction of the energy is stored in the biomass and passed on to the next level.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Ecological Efficiency:**

 
 
• Ecological efficiency refers to the percentage of energy transferred from one trophic level to another.
 
• It is generally low, around **5-20%**, depending on the ecosystem.
 
 
 
• **Implications of Energy Loss:**
 
 
• The loss of energy at each trophic level explains why food chains are usually limited to **3-5 levels**.
 
• Higher trophic levels have less energy available, leading to fewer organisms at the top of the pyramid.
 
 
 
• **Real-World Examples:**
 
 
• In a grassland ecosystem, grass captures solar energy, herbivores (like deer) consume grass, and carnivores (like lions) prey on herbivores.
 
• Energy decreases significantly as it moves from grass to herbivores to carnivores.

The correct answer is __**Kapil**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Sankhya system of philosophy** is one of the six classical schools of Indian philosophy and is credited to **Kapil**, an ancient Indian sage.
 
• Sankhya philosophy is a **dualistic system** that distinguishes between **Purusha (consciousness or soul)** and **Prakriti (matter or nature)**.
 
• Kapil is considered the **founder of Sankhya philosophy**, which emphasizes the importance of knowledge and self-awareness for liberation or **Moksha**.
 
• Sankhya philosophy primarily focuses on understanding the **cosmic evolution** and the interaction between Purusha and Prakriti.
 
• The Sankhya system profoundly influenced other schools of Indian philosophy, such as **Yoga**, and is regarded as one of the oldest philosophical systems in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kapil:**

 
 
• Kapil is regarded as a **historical figure** and a sage from ancient India who introduced Sankhya philosophy.
 
• His teachings are preserved in various texts, including the **Sankhya Karika**, which outlines the principles of Sankhya philosophy.
 
• He is often described in Indian scriptures as a sage with profound knowledge of metaphysics and spiritual sciences.
 
• Kapil’s insights laid the foundation for understanding the relationship between **consciousness and material existence**.
 
 
 
• **Sankhya Philosophy:**
 
 
• It is one of the **six orthodox schools** of Indian philosophy, alongside Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa, and Vedanta.
 
• The term "Sankhya" literally translates to **"number" or "enumeration"**, as the philosophy categorizes the various elements of existence.
 
• Sankhya identifies **25 tattvas** (principles), including Purusha, Prakriti, intellect, ego, mind, and the five elements.
 
• It is a **non-theistic philosophy**, focusing on self-realization rather than worship of a deity.
 
 
 
• **Other Philosophers Mentioned:**
 
 
• **Vyas:** He is traditionally credited as the compiler of the **Mahabharata** and the **Vedanta Sutras**. He is not associated with Sankhya philosophy.
 
• **Kanad:** He is the founder of the **Vaisheshika school** of Indian philosophy, which deals with atomism and metaphysics.
 
• **Gautam:** He is the founder of the **Nyaya philosophy**, which focuses on logic and epistemology.
 
 
 
• **Influence of Sankhya Philosophy:**
 
 
• Sankhya philosophy forms the theoretical backbone of **Yoga philosophy**, which incorporates its metaphysical concepts.
 
• It has contributed to the development of spiritual practices aimed at achieving **liberation (Moksha)** through self-awareness.
 
• Its dualistic perspective is considered a cornerstone in understanding the nature of reality in Indian philosophical traditions.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Context:** Sankhya philosophy is considered one of the **oldest philosophical systems** in India, predating texts like the **Upanishads**.
 
• **Core Concepts:** The dualistic concept of **Purusha and Prakriti** is central to understanding cosmic evolution and spiritual progress in Sankhya.
 
• **Practical Application:** The principles of Sankhya were later integrated into Yoga, providing a practical framework for achieving **spiritual liberation**.

questions.question: Which of the following dynasties patronised the construction of the Kailashnath temple at Ellora?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Kailashnath Temple** at Ellora is a remarkable example of ancient Indian rock-cut architecture and is located in the **Aurangabad district of Maharashtra**.
 
• The temple was commissioned by the **Rashtrakuta dynasty** under the reign of **King Krishna I** in the 8th century CE.
 
• It is dedicated to **Lord Shiva** and represents Mount Kailash, the abode of Lord Shiva, which is why it is named "Kailashnath."
 
• The temple is a monolithic structure, carved out of a single rock, showcasing remarkable engineering and artistic skills of the time.
 
• The Rashtrakutas are known for their patronage of art and architecture, and the Kailashnath Temple stands as a testament to their dedication to cultural advancement.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Rashtrakuta Dynasty:**

 
 
• The Rashtrakutas ruled large parts of the Indian subcontinent between the **6th and 10th centuries CE**.
 
• Their empire extended from the **Narmada River in the north to the Kaveri River in the south**.
 
• The Rashtrakutas were great patrons of art, literature, and architecture, and their reign is often considered a golden period of Indian culture.
 
• They also encouraged Jainism and Buddhism, as evidenced by the rock-cut caves at Ellora and other sites.
 
 
 
• **Kailashnath Temple:**
 
 
• It is part of the **Ellora Caves**, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, which includes a total of 34 caves representing Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain traditions.
 
• The Kailashnath Temple is cave number 16 at Ellora and is one of the largest rock-cut temples in the world.
 
• The construction involved the removal of approximately **200,000 tons of rock**, which was done using primitive tools like chisels and hammers.
 
• The temple features intricate carvings depicting scenes from the **Ramayana, Mahabharata**, and other Hindu epics.
 
 
 
• **Other Dynasties Mentioned:**
 
 
• **Chaulukya:** Also known as the Solankis, they ruled parts of western India, particularly Gujarat, from the 10th to 13th centuries CE.
 
• **Gupta:** The Gupta Empire (4th-6th centuries CE) is known as the "Golden Age of India" due to significant advancements in science, technology, art, and literature. They did not contribute to the construction of the Kailashnath Temple.
 
• **Solanki:** A branch of the Chaulukya dynasty, they were prominent in Gujarat and Rajasthan, known for their architectural contributions like the Modhera Sun Temple.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Kailashnath Temple:**
 
 
• It exemplifies the advanced technology and artistic skills of ancient Indian craftsmen.
 
• The temple is a symbol of devotion, representing the cultural and religious values of the time.
 
• It continues to attract tourists and scholars from around the world, serving as an important site for historical and architectural studies.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Ellora Caves:**

 
 
• The Ellora Caves are located near Aurangabad, Maharashtra, and consist of 34 caves, including Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain monuments.
 
• The Rashtrakutas primarily contributed to the Hindu caves, while the earlier caves were Buddhist, and the later ones were Jain.
 
 
 
• **Architectural Techniques:**
 
 
• The monolithic structure was carved top-down, which required remarkable planning and precision.
 
• The carvings and sculptures were made directly into the rock using chisels and other tools, showcasing the artisans' skills.
 
 
 
• **Legacy of the Rashtrakutas:**
 
 
• The Rashtrakutas left behind a legacy of cultural and architectural achievements that have greatly influenced Indian art and architecture.
 
• They are remembered for their patronage of scholars, poets, and artists.

• When **Baking soda solution** reacts with China Rose indicator, it gives a **green color**, indicating its basic nature.
 
• China Rose indicator changes to **dark pink or magenta** in acidic solutions and **green** in basic solutions, making it a reliable indicator for distinguishing acid-base properties.
 
• Other indicators such as **Phenolphthalein**, **Turmeric**, and **Methyl Orange** provide different color changes in basic or acidic mediums, but they do not produce green color with baking soda solution.

• Phenolphthalein is a commonly used indicator in acid-base titrations.
 
• It remains **colorless** in acidic solutions and turns **pink** in basic solutions.

• **Turmeric:**
 
 
• Turmeric contains curcumin, which acts as a natural indicator.
 
• It turns **reddish-brown** in basic solutions and remains yellow in acidic solutions.

• **Methyl Orange:**
 
 
• Methyl Orange is another acid-base indicator that produces **red** color in acidic solutions and **yellow** in basic solutions.
 
• It does not produce green color with baking soda solution.
 
 
 
• **China Rose:**
 
 
• China Rose acts as a natural indicator derived from the hibiscus flower.
 
• In acidic solutions, it changes to a **dark pink or magenta** color.
 
• In basic solutions, it changes to a **green color**, making it ideal for identifying basic substances like baking soda solution.

__
 
• The **sex ratio** in India refers to the number of females per 1,000 males. It is a crucial demographic indicator reflecting gender balance in the population.
 
• Between the 1901 and 1971 censuses, the **sex ratio in India continuously declined** due to various socio-economic and cultural factors.

• In the **1901 Census**, the sex ratio was **972 females per 1,000 males**.
 
• By **1941**, it had dropped to **945**, and further declined to **930** by the 1971 Census.
 
• The 1981 Census showed a slight improvement at **933 females per 1,000 males**, marking a reversal in the declining trend.
 
• In the **2001 Census**, the sex ratio rose to **933 females per 1,000 males**, showcasing sustained improvement.
 
 
 
• **Factors Influencing the Sex Ratio:**
 
 
• **Socio-cultural Practices**: Practices such as preference for male children and female infanticide historically contributed to a declining sex ratio.
 
• **Healthcare Improvements**: Better maternal and child healthcare services have contributed to reducing mortality rates among women and female children.
 
• **Education and Awareness**: Increased awareness and education about gender equality have played a role in improving the sex ratio.
 
• **Government Initiatives**: Campaigns such as **Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao** aim to tackle gender discrimination and improve the status of girls in society.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Gender Imbalance:**
 
 
• A skewed sex ratio can lead to social challenges, including increased violence against women and issues related to gender inequality.
 
• It can also result in a demographic imbalance, affecting marriage patterns and societal structures.
 
 
 
• **Measures to Improve the Sex Ratio:**
 
 
• Strict enforcement of laws prohibiting **prenatal sex determination** (e.g., the **Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act**).
 
• Promotion of gender equality through education and awareness campaigns.
 
• Provision of financial incentives for families with girl children through schemes like the **Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana**.

__
 
• The rate of increase in temperature with depth in the **upper crust of Earth** is known as the **geothermal gradient**.
 
• On average, the geothermal gradient is about **30°C per kilometre** in the Earth's upper crust, though this value can vary depending on the region and local geological conditions.
 
• The geothermal gradient is higher in regions with **active tectonic plate boundaries** or volcanic activities due to increased geothermal energy in such areas.
 
• The Earth's internal heat primarily originates from the **radioactive decay of elements** like uranium, thorium, and potassium, along with residual heat from the Earth's formation.
 
• This temperature gradient plays a critical role in processes like the generation of **magma**, the formation of **metamorphic rocks**, and the movement of **hydrothermal fluids**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Geothermal Gradient:**

 
 
• The geothermal gradient refers to the **rate at which temperature increases with depth** inside the Earth.
 
• It generally ranges between **20°C and 40°C per kilometre** in most of the Earth's crust.
 
• In areas with active volcanic or tectonic activity, this gradient may exceed 40°C per kilometre, while in stable continental interiors, it may be lower.
 
 
 
• **Earth’s Internal Heat Sources:**
 
 
• The primary sources of Earth's internal heat are:
 
 
• **Radioactive decay:** The decay of radioactive isotopes like uranium-238, thorium-232, and potassium-40 generates significant heat.
 
• **Residual heat:** Heat remaining from the Earth's formation approximately **4.5 billion years ago**.
 
• **Frictional heat:** Heat generated by the movement of tectonic plates.
 
 
 
 
 
• **Applications of Geothermal Gradient:**
 
 
• **Geothermal energy:** The geothermal gradient is harnessed in certain regions to generate renewable energy for heating and electricity.
 
• **Oil and gas exploration:** Knowledge of the geothermal gradient helps in predicting the maturity of hydrocarbon resources.
 
• **Geological studies:** It aids in understanding crustal and mantle processes, including plate tectonics and magma generation.
 
 
 
• **Variation of Geothermal Gradient:**
 
 
• The geothermal gradient is not uniform across the Earth and is influenced by factors like:
 
 
• **Crustal thickness:** Thicker crust tends to have a lower gradient.
 
• **Heat flow:** Areas with higher heat flow (e.g., near mid-ocean ridges or hotspots) have steeper gradients.
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Geothermal Energy Potential:**

 
 
• Regions with a high geothermal gradient, such as **Iceland, New Zealand, and parts of the United States (Yellowstone National Park)**, are often used for geothermal energy production.
 
• Geothermal energy is considered a **renewable and sustainable energy source**, as Earth's heat is virtually inexhaustible over human time scales.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Mining:**
 
 
• Understanding the geothermal gradient is crucial in **deep mining operations**, as increasing temperatures can pose challenges to working conditions and equipment.

__
 
• **Bhaona** is a traditional **theatre form** of Assam, which was introduced by the great Vaishnavite saint and social reformer, **Sankaradeva**, during the 16th century.
 
• Bhaona performances are based on episodes from the **Bhagavata Purana** and other Hindu scriptures, particularly focusing on the themes of devotion and morality.
 
• The performances are conducted in the **namghar** (prayer hall) and are a crucial element of the Neo-Vaishnavite movement in Assam, which sought to spread the message of devotion and equality.
 
• It is characterized by elaborate costumes, synchronized dance moves, and soulful singing, accompanied by traditional musical instruments like the **khol** (drum) and **tala** (cymbals).
 
• The dialogues of the performances are usually in the Assamese language, interspersed with verses from Sanskrit.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Origin and Purpose:**

 
 
• Bhaona was created as a medium to educate and entertain the masses about religious teachings and ethical living.
 
• Sankaradeva designed it to be accessible to the common people, making religious texts and ideas relatable and engaging.
 
 
 
• **Key Elements of Bhaona:**
 
 
• **Music:** The musical component includes devotional songs like **Borgeet**, composed by Sankaradeva and his disciple Madhavdeva.
 
• **Costumes:** Artists wear ornate costumes, including crowns, jewelry, and colorful attire, to depict deities, demons, and other characters.
 
• **Instruments:** Instruments like the **khol**, **tala**, and **mridanga** are used to complement the performance.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Art Forms:**
 
 
• Bhaona is distinct from puppet forms or festivals because it involves live actors performing on stage with dialogues and elaborate expressions.
 
• It is not a musical instrument but incorporates music as an integral part of the performance.
 
 
 
• **Modern Relevance:**
 
 
• Bhaona continues to be an essential part of Assamese culture and is performed during religious and cultural festivals.
 
• Efforts have been made to preserve this art form by including it in cultural programs and school curriculums in Assam.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Other Traditional Art Forms of Assam:**

 
 
• **Sattriya:** A classical dance form of Assam, also developed by Sankaradeva, which is closely associated with Bhaona.
 
• **Bihu:** A folk dance performed during the Assamese New Year, representing joy and celebration.
 
• **Ojapali:** A semi-dramatic performance that combines singing, dancing, and storytelling, often focusing on mythological tales.
 
 
 
• **Recognition:**
 
 
• Bhaona and other art forms of Assam have gained attention on national and international platforms due to their cultural and historical significance.

questions.question: Which of the following lakes is formed in a depression which is said to have been formed due to a meteorite?

__
 
• **Lonar Lake** is a unique saltwater lake located in the **Buldhana district of Maharashtra**, India. It was formed due to a **meteorite impact** that occurred approximately **50,000 years ago**.
 
• The lake is classified as a **hyper-velocity impact crater**, making it one of the rarest geological formations in the world and the only one of its kind in basaltic rock.
 
• Lonar Lake is nearly circular in shape, measuring around **1.2 kilometers in diameter**, and is surrounded by a rim of ejecta, which is a characteristic feature of meteorite impact craters.
 
• The lake has both scientific and ecological significance due to its unique water chemistry, which includes a mix of **alkaline and saline water**, supporting microorganisms and biodiversity not commonly found elsewhere.
 
• The site has attracted geologists, ecologists, and astronomers for research purposes. Studies have confirmed the meteoritic origin of the crater through **petrological and geochemical analyses**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Formation of Lonar Lake:**

 
 
• The lake was formed when a **meteorite weighing approximately 2 million tons** collided with the Earth at a speed of around **90,000 km/h**, creating the crater.
 
• This impact led to the excavation of basaltic rock, which is a characteristic feature of the **Deccan Plateau region**.
 
• The crater walls and ejecta contain minerals like **maskelynite**, which is formed due to high-velocity impacts.
 
 
 
• **Scientific Importance:**
 
 
• The lake's ecosystem is highly unique, consisting of both **alkaline water** in the main lake and freshwater in the surrounding springs.
 
• Microbial studies have revealed extremophiles thriving in the harsh chemical environment of the lake, contributing to advancements in microbiology.
 
• The lake's unique geology has been studied by **NASA and Geological Survey of India** for its resemblance to lunar and Martian craters.
 
 
 
• **Tourist Attraction:**
 
 
• Lonar Lake is a popular destination for tourists and nature enthusiasts due to its historical temples like the **Daitya Sudan temple**, which are built near the lake.
 
• The site is also revered in mythology, with references in ancient texts like the **Skanda Purana**.

• **Sambhar Lake:** Located in Rajasthan, it is India's largest inland saltwater lake. It is renowned for salt production but is not formed due to a meteorite impact.
 
• **Loktak Lake:** Located in Manipur, it is famous for its floating islands called **phumdis**. It is a freshwater lake with ecological significance, unrelated to meteorite activity.
 
• **Hussain Sagar Lake:** Situated in Hyderabad, it is an artificial lake built during the reign of **Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah in 1563**. It has no connection to meteorite impacts.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Lonar Lake Conservation:**

 
 
• The lake is designated as a **National Geo-Heritage Monument** by the Geological Survey of India, highlighting its importance for geological preservation.
 
• Efforts are being made to protect its unique ecosystem from pollution and human interference.
 
 
 
• **Global Significance:**
 
 
• Lonar Lake is one of the few sites on Earth where scientists can study the effects of meteorite impacts on basaltic rock, making it invaluable for planetary science.
 
• Its study provides insights into similar craters found on the Moon and Mars, aiding space exploration research.
 
 
 
• **Historical References:**
 
 
• The lake has been mentioned in ancient Indian literature and was first scientifically documented by British officer **C. J. E. Alexander** in 1823.
 
• It continues to be a site of cultural, historical, and scientific importance.

__
 
• The **Punchhi Commission** was set up in **2007** under the chairmanship of **Madan Mohan Punchhi**, a former Chief Justice of India, to examine and recommend changes for a better framework of **Centre-State Relations**.
 
• The commission submitted its report in **2010**, addressing various issues related to the **division of powers** between the Centre and the states in India.
 
• It extensively studied the provisions of the **Constitution of India**, particularly those related to federalism and the distribution of legislative and administrative powers.
 
• The commission recommended measures to ensure a balance between **state autonomy** and the need for a strong Centre to address national concerns.
 
• Key recommendations included reforms in areas like the **appointment of Governors, emergency provisions, financial relations, and inter-state disputes** to enhance coordination and minimize conflicts between the Centre and States.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Centre-State Relations:**

 
 
• The relationship between the Centre and States in India is governed by the **Constitution**, which provides for a **three-tier system of government** - Union, State, and Local.
 
• It includes **legislative, administrative, and financial relations**, with specific lists under the **7th Schedule** such as the Union List, State List, and Concurrent List.
 
• **Article 246** and the division of powers between the Union and States play a crucial role in governance.
 
• The **Inter-State Council**, established under **Article 263**, is an important forum for resolving disputes and fostering cooperation.
 
 
 
• **Punchhi Commission Recommendations:**
 
 
• Governors should act impartially and avoid being involved in politically controversial matters.
 
• Emergency provisions under **Articles 352, 356, and 360** should be used sparingly and only in exceptional circumstances.
 
• Financial relations between the Centre and States should be reviewed to ensure equitable distribution of resources.
 
• Mechanisms to resolve **inter-state disputes**, especially water sharing conflicts, should be strengthened.
 
 
 
• **Important Articles Related to Centre-State Relations:**
 
 
• **Article 280:** Establishes the **Finance Commission** to recommend the distribution of financial resources between the Centre and States.
 
• **Article 256:** States must comply with the laws made by Parliament and not impede their implementation.
 
• **Article 262:** Provides for the adjudication of disputes relating to waters of inter-state rivers or river valleys.
 
• **Article 368:** Empowers Parliament to amend the Constitution, including provisions related to Centre-State relations.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Federal System in India:**

 
 
• India follows a **quasi-federal structure**, where the Centre holds more powers compared to States.
 
• The Constitution has provisions for **cooperative federalism**, ensuring collaboration between different levels of government.
 
• The **Supreme Court of India** acts as the guardian of federal balance and resolves disputes between the Centre and States.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• The **Sarkaria Commission**, set up in **1983**, was the first major effort to examine Centre-State relations comprehensively.
 
• The **Punchhi Commission** built upon the Sarkaria Commission’s findings to address new challenges in the Indian federal system.

questions.question: Which of the following is also called the 'suicide bag' of a cell?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lysosome**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Lysosomes** are often referred to as the "suicide bags" of a cell because they contain hydrolytic enzymes capable of breaking down cellular components.
 
• These enzymes are used for the digestion and recycling of cellular waste, damaged organelles, and macromolecules.
 
• Lysosomes play a crucial role in programmed cell death (apoptosis), where their enzymes are released to degrade the cell internally.
 
• They are typically found in animal cells and are formed by the **Golgi apparatus**, which packages the hydrolytic enzymes into vesicles.
 
• The internal environment of lysosomes is highly acidic (pH ~4.5-5), which is optimal for the activity of their digestive enzymes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **DNA:**

 
 
• DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid) is the genetic material found in the nucleus of a cell.
 
• It is responsible for storing and transmitting genetic information for protein synthesis and inheritance.
 
• DNA does not play a role in digestion or apoptosis; hence, it is not referred to as the "suicide bag" of the cell.
 
 
 
• **Golgi Apparatus:**
 
 
• The Golgi apparatus is involved in modifying, sorting, and packaging proteins and lipids for secretion or use within the cell.
 
• It plays a role in lysosome formation by packaging hydrolytic enzymes into vesicles.
 
• However, it is not directly involved in cellular digestion or apoptosis.
 
 
 
• **Mitochondria:**
 
 
• Mitochondria are known as the "powerhouses" of the cell, as they generate energy in the form of ATP through cellular respiration.
 
• They are not involved in cellular digestion or the destruction of cellular components.
 
• Mitochondria play a role in apoptosis but are not called "suicide bags."
 
 
 
• **Lysosome Function:**
 
 
• Lysosomes are responsible for intracellular digestion, recycling cellular components, and defending the cell against pathogens.
 
• They degrade biological molecules such as proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and carbohydrates.
 
• Defects in lysosomal enzymes can lead to lysosomal storage disorders, such as Tay-Sachs disease.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Discovery:** Lysosomes were discovered by **Christian de Duve** in **1955**.
 
• **Enzymes:** They contain hydrolytic enzymes like proteases, lipases, nucleases, and carbohydrases.
 
• **Diseases:** Malfunctioning lysosomes can lead to disorders like Gaucher's disease and Niemann-Pick disease.
 
• **Cellular Defense:** Lysosomes help to destroy pathogens engulfed by the cell during phagocytosis.

questions.question: How many members does the RBI’s Monetary Policy Committee have?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Six**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** of the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** comprises **six members**. This is mandated under the **RBI Act, 1934**.
 
• Out of the six members, **three are officials from the RBI**, including the Governor of the RBI, who acts as the **Chairperson of the MPC**.
 
• The other **three members are external experts**, nominated by the Government of India. These members are selected based on their expertise in economics, banking, or finance.
 
• The MPC is responsible for setting the **policy interest rates**, specifically the **repo rate**, to achieve inflation targets and ensure economic stability.
 
• The decisions of the MPC are made by a **majority vote**. Each member has one vote, and in case of a tie, the RBI Governor has the **casting vote**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Functions of the Monetary Policy Committee:**

 
 
• The MPC is tasked with formulating the **Monetary Policy** of India, including setting the **repo rate** (the rate at which banks borrow from the RBI).
 
• The committee aims to maintain **price stability** while keeping in mind the objective of economic growth.
 
• The inflation target is determined by the Government of India, and the MPC ensures that inflation remains within the prescribed limits (currently, the target is **4% with a +/- 2% tolerance band**).
 
 
 
• **Composition of the MPC:**
 
 
• The **RBI Governor** serves as the Chairperson of the committee.
 
• The **Deputy Governor of RBI**, who is in charge of monetary policy, is also a member.
 
• The **Executive Director of the RBI**, overseeing monetary policy, is the third RBI member.
 
• The Government nominates three **independent members**, who are eminent economists and professionals.
 
 
 
• **Decision-Making Process:**
 
 
• The MPC meets **bi-monthly** to review the monetary policy.
 
• Each member of the MPC has one vote, and the decisions are taken by **majority voting.**
 
• In case of a tie in voting, the **RBI Governor** has the casting vote.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• The MPC was established in **2016**, replacing the earlier system where the RBI Governor solely decided on monetary policy.
 
• The change aimed to bring transparency and accountability to the monetary policy framework.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Inflation Targeting:**

 
 
• The MPC’s primary role is to achieve the **inflation target** set by the Government of India. Currently, the target is **4%** with a tolerance band of **+/- 2%**.
 
• The inflation target is reviewed every **five years**.
 
 
 
• **Significance of MPC:**
 
 
• The MPC ensures a balanced approach to monetary policy by involving **external experts**, reducing the chances of bias.
 
• It enhances **transparency** and credibility in the monetary policy-making process.
 
• The bi-monthly meetings and their outcomes are **publicly disclosed** to maintain accountability.
 
 
 
• **Recent Trends:**
 
 
• The MPC has been instrumental in maintaining inflation within the target range amid global challenges like **COVID-19** and geopolitical tensions.
 
• It has also played a pivotal role in ensuring **liquidity** in the financial markets during economic downturns.

questions.question: In the context of Chola administration, the term 'vetti' meant ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**tax**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The term **'vetti'** was widely used in the administrative system of the **Chola Dynasty** to denote a form of tax or levy imposed on the people.
 
• **Vetti** often referred to a type of tax that could be collected in kind or labor, particularly from the agrarian society that formed the backbone of the Chola economy.
 
• The Chola rulers maintained an efficient administrative system, and taxes like **'vetti'** helped fund projects such as temple construction, irrigation systems, and military campaigns.
 
• **'Vetti'** was sometimes considered a form of forced labor or tribute, reflecting the agrarian and feudal nature of the Chola administration.
 
• The collection of **'vetti'** was regulated and often overseen by local village assemblies, which played a significant role in governance during the Chola period.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Chola Administration:**

 
 
• The Chola Dynasty, which flourished between the 9th and 13th centuries CE, is known for its well-organized administrative structure.
 
• It had a decentralized system where local assemblies, known as **'sabhas'** or **'ur'**, played a crucial role in governance.
 
• The administration was divided into various units such as **provinces (mandalams)**, districts (nadus), and villages.
 
 
 
• **Types of Taxes:**
 
 
• The Chola rulers imposed various taxes, including land revenue, trade taxes, and labor taxes like **'vetti'**.
 
• The revenue from these taxes was used for public welfare projects such as the construction of temples and irrigation systems.
 
• Some taxes were paid in cash, while others like **'vetti'** could be paid through labor or goods.
 
 
 
• **Forced Labor:**
 
 
• **'Vetti'** was sometimes equated with forced labor, where individuals had to provide services to the state or local authorities.
 
• This system of taxation was common in agrarian societies to ensure labor for public works.
 
 
 
• **Village Assemblies:**
 
 
• Village assemblies or **'sabhas'** were responsible for managing local affairs, including tax collection, dispute resolution, and maintenance of public resources.
 
• These assemblies were composed of members from various strata of society and operated democratically.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Chola Temples:**

 
 
• The revenue collected through taxes like **'vetti'** was often used for the construction and maintenance of grand temples, such as the **Brihadeshwara Temple** in Tamil Nadu.
 
• These temples served as centers of culture, religion, and economic activity during the Chola period.
 
 
 
• **Irrigation Systems:**
 
 
• The Chola rulers utilized tax revenue to build and maintain extensive irrigation systems, ensuring agricultural prosperity.
 
• These systems included canals, tanks, and wells, showcasing advanced engineering skills.
 
 
 
• **Military Campaigns:**
 
 
• Taxes like **'vetti'** funded the Chola military, enabling them to expand their territory and establish dominance over South India and parts of Southeast Asia.

questions.question: In whose court did Heliodorus come as an ambassador during second century BCE?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bhagabhadra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Heliodorus** was a Greek ambassador who came to the court of **Bhagabhadra**, a ruler of the Shunga dynasty in **second century BCE**.
 
• Heliodorus was sent by the Greek king **Antialkidas**, who ruled over Taxila during that period.
 
• Heliodorus is famously known for erecting the **Heliodorus pillar**, also called the "Garuda Pillar," at **Vidisha (Madhya Pradesh)**. This pillar stands as evidence of the cultural and religious interactions between the Greeks and Indians.
 
• The inscription on the pillar states that Heliodorus was a follower of **Vishnu**, marking one of the earliest records of foreign devotion to Hinduism.
 
• The Shunga dynasty, under Bhagabhadra's rule, is noted for its contributions to Indian culture, including art, architecture, and religious developments.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Heliodorus Pillar:**

 
 
• The pillar was erected in **113 BCE** and contains inscriptions in Brahmi script.
 
• It has an inscription referring to Heliodorus as the "devotee of Vishnu" and describes him as a Greek (Yavana).
 
• The pillar highlights the spread of **Vaishnavism** during the Shunga dynasty and its acceptance by foreign dignitaries.
 
 
 
• **Shunga Dynasty:**
 
 
• The Shunga dynasty ruled from **185 BCE to 73 BCE** and succeeded the Mauryan dynasty.
 
• It was established by **Pushyamitra Shunga**, a former Mauryan general.
 
• The dynasty is known for its patronage of **Hinduism** and contributions to art and architecture, including the development of stupas like the **Sanchi Stupa**.
 
 
 
• **Antialkidas:**
 
 
• Antialkidas was a **Indo-Greek king** who ruled over the region of Taxila.
 
• His reign was marked by diplomatic relations with Indian rulers, as evidenced by the embassy of Heliodorus.
 
• The Indo-Greeks are noted for their cultural syncretism, blending Greek and Indian traditions.
 
 
 
• **Vidisha:**
 
 
• Vidisha, located in modern-day Madhya Pradesh, served as an important center of trade and culture during the Shunga period.
 
• It was a hub for religious activities, including the construction of stupas and pillars, and saw significant interaction between Indian and foreign cultures.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Religious and Cultural Exchange:**

 
 
• The interaction between Indo-Greeks and Indian rulers, as seen in the case of Heliodorus, showcases the mutual respect and exchange of religious and cultural practices.
 
• Heliodorus' devotion to Vishnu highlights the spread of Hinduism beyond Indian territories and its acceptance by foreigners.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Inscriptions:**
 
 
• Historical inscriptions like the one on the Heliodorus pillar are crucial for understanding the socio-political and religious dynamics of ancient India.
 
• They provide insights into the relations between Indian kingdoms and foreign powers, as well as the spread of Indian religions and philosophies.

questions.question: Who among the following has NEVER been a speaker of Lok Sabha?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pratibha Patil**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pratibha Patil** was the **12th President of India** and the first woman to hold this prestigious office from **2007 to 2012**. She has **never served as the Speaker of the Lok Sabha**.
 
• **PA Sangma** was a prominent Indian politician from Meghalaya and served as the **Speaker of the Lok Sabha** from **1996 to 1998**. Hence, he has held this position.
 
• **Balram Jakhar** was the Speaker of the Lok Sabha from **1980 to 1989**. He was the longest-serving Speaker of the Lok Sabha in Indian history. Therefore, he was indeed a Speaker.
 
• **Somnath Chatterjee**, a respected parliamentarian, served as the Speaker of the Lok Sabha from **2004 to 2009**. He played a crucial role in parliamentary debates and discussions.
 
• **Pratibha Patil**, unlike the other mentioned individuals, has **never held the position of Speaker of the Lok Sabha**. Her contributions were primarily in the executive branch as President, not the legislative branch.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Speaker of the Lok Sabha:**

 
 
• The Speaker is the **presiding officer** of the Lok Sabha, the lower house of Parliament in India.
 
• The Speaker is responsible for conducting sessions of the Lok Sabha, maintaining decorum, and deciding on procedural matters.
 
• Some notable Speakers include **Ganesh Vasudev Mavalankar** (first Speaker), **Meira Kumar** (first woman Speaker), and **Om Birla** (current Speaker as of 2023).
 
 
 
• **Pratibha Patil:**
 
 
• She served as the **Governor of Rajasthan** before becoming the President of India.
 
• Pratibha Patil was the first woman President of India, serving from **July 25, 2007, to July 25, 2012**.
 
• Her presidency was marked by her focus on social welfare, education, and women empowerment.
 
 
 
• **Other notable Speakers:**
 
 
• **Balram Jakhar:** Known for his contributions to parliamentary procedures and agricultural reforms.
 
• **Somnath Chatterjee:** Renowned for his impartiality and strong defense of parliamentary ethics.
 
• **PA Sangma:** Played a significant role in debates and discussions during his tenure as Speaker.
 
 
 
• **Key Functions of the Speaker:**
 
 
• Ensuring smooth functioning of the Lok Sabha.
 
• Representing the Lok Sabha in all its capacities.
 
• Maintaining order during debates and discussions.
 
• Deciding on matters of privilege and procedural issues.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Eligibility for Speaker:**

 
 
• The Speaker must be a **member of the Lok Sabha**.
 
• He/she is elected by the members of the Lok Sabha.
 
• The Speaker serves until the dissolution of the Lok Sabha or resignation/removal.
 
 
 
• **Unique Contributions:**
 
 
• **Pratibha Patil:** Focused on inclusivity and women empowerment during her presidency.
 
• **Balram Jakhar:** Played a crucial role in agricultural reforms and parliamentary efficiency.
 
• **Somnath Chatterjee:** Advocated for ethical parliamentary practices.
